title: The Sweetest Thing
full_review:
"The Sweetest Thing" (Columbia) is actually quite sour. Its painfully stupid plot is a thinly veiled excuse to have the female leads parade around in their underwear. And because it's got a star name in the lead, Cameron Diaz, moviegoers might be fooled into thinking it's worth the price of admission. But viewers are likely to be sorely disappointed as Diaz's small dose of charm fades away almost as soon as the opening credits finish.

Diaz plays sassy, twentysomething single, Christina Walters, living in San Francisco. Christina's golden rule of dating is "don't look for Mr. Right, look for Mr. Right Now." An amusing opening montage shows her former beaux describing what a cold heart-breaker she is. This is about as funny as "South Park" writer Nancy M. Pimental's script gets as her stale writing can't seem to muster up even one original line or joke.

Christina spends her life club hopping with her roommates, Courtney (Christina Applegate), an improbable divorce lawyer who dresses in the latest fashions from Frederick's of Hollywood, and the recently dumped Jane (Selma Blair). It is on one such outing that she unexpectedly meets Peter (Thomas Jane), in town with his brother (Jason Bateman) for a wedding in an affluent Northern California suburb. He confronts Christina for calling him a name and she becomes smitten, seemingly attracted to a guy who can dish it out as well as she can. But afraid to make the next move, she lets him disappear without getting his phone number. The only way she can track him down is to drive three hours up the coast and crash the wedding. Before the audience can plead for mercy, the film turns into a buddy road movie, complete with a pit stop at a gross roadside bathroom.

It should be mortifying to the filmmakers that script doesn't have enough material to sustain its 84-minute running time. Stuffed with more fillers than a hot dog, the movie seemed to be written in a morning and shot in an afternoon. It is poor indeed when a movie needs to include a "movie montage" where the protagonists dress up and play out scenes from famous films to fill time. The dialogue is brimming with trash talk and several crass scenes, one at a dry cleaners involving a stained dress (think Monica Lewinsky) that pulls in a bunch of stereotypical Chinese and Irish characters. Abstinence is certainly not a thought to these "Sex in the City" wannabes, and marriage and commitment are once again the butt of jokes.

Over-the-top acting is a result of Kumble's lazy directing style. He also does nothing with the beautiful San Francisco locale, shooting scenes as if they were in some studio back lot.

"The Sweetest Thing" is no treat.

Because of several sexual situations and explicit references, partial nudity and recurring rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
